subject: English
passage: The Alchemist is a 1610 play by Ben Jonson, originally written in early modern English. At the time, practitioners called alchemists offered paying clients promises of transmuting base metals into gold and sometimes conducted what they described as natural philosophy. Jonson satirizes alchemists' practices and views as foolish, as seen when the character ______
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses a quotation from The Alchemist to illustrate the claim?

choices.A: Mammon, after consulting with an alchemist, says to his companion, "Come on, sir. Now you set your foot on shore in novo orbe; here's the rich Peru: and there within, sir, are the golden mines."
choices.B: Subtle, an alchemist, says to a prospective client, "Pray you, sit down; and let me know your business plainly and at once."
choices.C: Mammon urges his friend to hire an alchemist, saying, "If you would have your fortune made entire, entrust yourself to this man's keeping wholly."
choices.D: Subtle, an alchemist, explains why he must pour his elixir into a flask buried beneath horse dung, saying, "The heat of the dung, being gentle and maternal, doth nurse the embryo of our stone, and quicken into perfection what the fire alone would burn to nothing."

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it most effectively uses a quotation to illustrate the claim that Jonson satirizes alchemists' practices and views as foolish. In the quotation, Subtle, identified as an alchemist, explains that he must bury his elixir beneath horse dung because the 'gentle and maternal' heat 'doth nurse the embryo of our stone.' The ludicrous image of a serious practitioner burying his materials in manure, combined with grandiose pseudo-scientific language about nursing an 'embryo,' effectively portrays alchemists' practices as absurd and pretentious.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect because the quotation doesn't satirize alchemists' practices or views as foolish. While it does show Subtle, an alchemist, speaking to a prospective client, what he says—politely asking the client to sit and state his business—is a straightforward, reasonable request that doesn't present alchemical practice as absurd.
